newsitem.title: CHINA: No crackdown for handover protest in new Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: No crackdown for handover protest in new Hong Kong.

text.p: Chinese-ruled Hong Kong sought to show political tolerance on Thursday by ruling out action against groups who staged a defiant pro-democracy protest on the balcony of parliament on handover night.
Hong Kong's new Provisional Legislature issued a statement rebuking former legislators for a "regrettable" action but it promised to seek no punishment.
The protest occurred after midnight on Monday, when 156 years of British rule ended and China resumed sovereignty over this capitalist enclave of 6.4 million people.

Martin Lee, a lawyer and voice of democracy in the former British colony, mounted the Legislative Council balcony in downtown Hong Kong with his Democratic Party colleagues and addressed thousands of demonstrators in the square below.
Lee read out a declaration protesting against the elected legislature's disbandment and replacement by the China-appointed interim body, and vowing to fight for re-election.
The new legislature said it had reviewed the incident at a committee meeting on Thursday and decided not to pursue it.
"The meeting regretted the unauthorised action of this group, and strongly reprimanded their irresponsible way of operation," it said in a statement to media.
The protest was considered illegal under controversial laws passed by the Provisional Legislature on Tuesday.
Inspired by China several months ago, the laws set curbs on protests, requiring prior permission from police. The laws were retroactive to midnight Monday.
The protest action was widely viewed as a test of the tolerance level of the China-vetted government led by Tung Chee-hwa, a former shipping tycoon.
Although Hong Kong enjoys a high degree of autonomy as a sepcial region of China under the handover deal, many here had feared communist-style repression after the change of flag.
On Wednesday, speaking at his first news conference since the sovereignty change, Tung ridiculed the protest.
But he took a lenient view and said the incident had failed to spoil Hong Kong's handover celebrations.
The Provisional Legislature's president Rita Fan was quoted by government radio as saying legal action against Lee and his colleagues would be a waste of public money.

"We do not intend to take legal action against them, because if we do...we will be incurring taxpayers' expenses, and we do not wish to incur more taxpayers' expenses to pursue this matter," she said.
